lead: A second-order linear ODE with variable coefficients often has no elementary closed-form solution. This unit shows how to classify its points and build power-series and Frobenius solutions, then uses those tools for Legendre polynomials and Bessel functions. After it you can solve standard series problems, use orthogonality, and apply Abel and Sturm theorems to zeros.
about: The unit moves from local classification to series methods and then to classical special functions. Chapter 3.1 decides whether a point is ordinary, regular singular or irregular. Chapter 3.2 builds power-series solutions at ordinary points, and 3.3 extends the same idea to regular singular points with the Frobenius method. Chapters 3.4 and 3.5 apply this to Legendre's and Bessel's equations, where the polynomial and Bessel solutions are orthogonal. Chapter 3.6 states the Sturm-Liouville form that explains that orthogonality with a weight, and 3.7 adds Abel's formula and the Sturm separation and comparison theorems for zeros.

chapters.idea: Classify each point x0 of a second-order linear ODE by how its coefficient functions behave there, because that choice picks the series method.
chapters.depth: Use standard form y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = 0. Define analytic at x0 as having a convergent Taylor series there. Ordinary point: P and Q analytic at x0. Singular point: not ordinary. Regular singular point: (x − x0)P(x) and (x − x0)²Q(x) have finite limits at x0, equivalently are analytic there. Irregular singular: singular but not regular. Some syllabi say regular point for ordinary point, and regular singularity for regular singular point. Include p0 = lim (x − x0)P and q0 = lim (x − x0)²Q for use in 3.3. Show quick classifications for Bessel at x = 0 and Legendre at x = ±1, without solving.

figure.title: Classifying x0
figure.aria: A flowchart starts with a point x0 and sends the ODE to ordinary point or to a regularity check for singular points.

chapters.example: Classify x = 0 and x = 1 for (x² − 1)y'' + xy' + y = 0. In standard form, P(x) = x/(x² − 1) and Q(x) = 1/(x² − 1). At x = 0 both are analytic, so x = 0 is an ordinary point. At x = 1, (x − 1)P(x) = x/(x + 1) and (x − 1)²Q(x) = (x − 1)/(x + 1), both analytic at x = 1; so x = 1 is a regular singular point. The point x = −1 is also regular singular.
chapters.trap: Calling x = 1 irregular only because P and Q blow up. Regularity asks whether (x − x0)P and (x − x0)²Q stay finite.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: second-order linear ODEs; basic Taylor series from calculus.
chapters.leave: Solving the ODE, indicial equation and recurrence are in 3.2 and 3.3.

chapters.idea: At an ordinary point x0, a solution is a power series y = Σ a_n (x − x0)^n, and substitution gives a recurrence for the coefficients.
chapters.depth: Cover the full method: assume y = Σ a_n(x − x0)^n, differentiate term by term, substitute, shift indices, equate the coefficient of each power to zero, and solve the recurrence. Initial values fix a0 = y(x0) and a1 = y'(x0). State the radius-of-convergence guarantee: at least the distance from x0 to the nearest singular point in the complex plane. Work one second-order example, including a recurrence that couples coefficients two steps apart. Some syllabi call this the Taylor series method. Do not cover regular singular points here.

figure.title: Power series at an ordinary point
figure.aria: A flowchart shows assuming a power series, substituting, shifting indices, getting a recurrence and using initial values.

chapters.example: Solve y'' − xy = 0 about x = 0 with y(0) = 1 and y'(0) = 0, up to the term x⁶. The recurrence gives a2 = 0, a3 = a0/6, a4 = a1/12 = 0, a5 = a2/20 = 0, a6 = a3/30 = 1/180. The solution begins y = 1 + x³/6 + x⁶/180 + ... .
chapters.trap: Forgetting to shift the index in x·Σ a_n x^n, and thinking a2 is free. Initial conditions fix only a0 and a1.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 ordinary points; Unit 2 second-order ODEs; Taylor series.
chapters.leave: Regular singular points and the indicial equation are in 3.3; orthogonality is in 3.6.

chapters.idea: At a regular singular point, a Frobenius series y = (x − x0)^r Σ a_n(x − x0)^n can produce a solution, with r found from the indicial equation.
chapters.depth: Derive the indicial equation r(r − 1) + p0r + q0 = 0, where p0 = lim (x − x0)P and q0 = lim (x − x0)²Q. Treat the three root cases: distinct roots not differing by an integer; distinct roots differing by an integer; equal roots. For the last two, state that the second solution may contain a logarithm, but do not derive the full log series. Solve the recurrence for the larger root in examples. Some syllabi call this the Frobenius method at a regular singularity.

figure.title: Frobenius method
figure.aria: A flowchart starts at a regular singular point, computes p0 and q0, forms the indicial equation, takes its roots, then uses a recurrence for the series.

nodes.label: Assume y = x^r Σ a_n x^n

chapters.example: Use the Frobenius method at x = 0 for 2x²y'' − xy' + (1 + x)y = 0. Find the indicial roots and the series for the larger root through x⁴. Here p0 = −1/2 and q0 = 1/2, so 2r² − 3r + 1 = 0, giving r = 1 and r = 1/2. For r = 1, y1 = x(1 − x/3 + x²/30 − x³/630 + ...).
chapters.trap: Putting r where n + r belongs in the recurrence, dropping a0 ≠ 0, or assuming the smaller root always gives an independent ordinary series.
chapters.leave: Legendre and Bessel applications are in 3.4 and 3.5; Sturm theory is in 3.6 and 3.7.

chapters.idea: Legendre's equation has a regular singular point at x = ±1, and its polynomial solutions P_n(x) are orthogonal on [−1, 1].
chapters.depth: Cover (1 − x²)y'' − 2xy' + n(n + 1)y = 0, with n a nonnegative integer. Classify x = 0 as ordinary and x = ±1 as regular singular. Give Rodrigues' formula P_n(x) = 1/(2^n n!) d^n/dx^n (x² − 1)^n. Derive P0, P1, P2, P3 and the recurrence (n + 1)P_{n+1} = (2n + 1)xP_n − nP_{n−1}. State orthogonality ∫_{−1}^{1} P_m(x)P_n(x) dx = 0 for m ≠ n, and norm ∫ P_n² dx = 2/(2n + 1). Mention parity: P_n has the same parity as n. Some syllabi call these Legendre functions of the first kind, but here they are polynomials.

figure.aria: Four curves on the interval from minus one to one show the first four Legendre polynomials.

chapters.example: Find P0, P1, P2 and P3 from Rodrigues' formula, and verify ∫_{−1}^{1} P1(x)P3(x) dx = 0. The polynomials are P0 = 1, P1 = x, P2 = (3x² − 1)/2, P3 = (5x³ − 3x)/2. Then the integral is 1/2 ∫_{−1}^{1} (5x⁴ − 3x²) dx = 1/2(2 − 2) = 0.
chapters.trap: Using weight x or interval [0, 1] for Legendre orthogonality. The weight is 1 and the interval is [−1, 1]. Also n must be a nonnegative integer for P_n.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 point classification; 3.2 power series; 3.3 Frobenius for behaviour at x = ±1.
chapters.leave: General Legendre functions, boundary-value applications, Bessel functions and general Sturm theory are in 3.5 and 3.6.

chapters.idea: Bessel's equation has a regular singular point at x = 0, and its first-kind solution J_ν is a Frobenius series with oscillatory zeros and weighted orthogonality.
chapters.depth: Cover x²y'' + xy' + (x² − ν²)y = 0 with ν ≥ 0. Frobenius gives indicial roots r = ±ν. Give J_ν(x) = Σ_{m=0}^{∞} (−1)^m/(m! Γ(m + ν + 1)) (x/2)^{2m+ν}. State J_{−n} = (−1)^n J_n for integer n. Give first terms and the main properties: derivative/recurrence relations such as d/dx[x^ν J_ν(x)] = x^ν J_{ν−1}(x); zeros; orthogonality ∫_0^a x J_ν(α_m x)J_ν(α_n x) dx = 0 for m ≠ n, where α_m are suitable zeros of J_ν. Mention the second-kind Y_ν only as the log case for integer ν. Some syllabi call J_ν Bessel function of the first kind.

figure.aria: Two oscillating curves show the first few series terms for Bessel J zero and J one.

chapters.example: From the Bessel series, write J0(x) and J1(x) through x⁵, and check J0(0) = 1 and J1(0) = 0. The series are J0(x) = 1 − x²/4 + x⁴/64 − x⁶/2304 + ... and J1(x) = x/2 − x³/16 + x⁵/384 + ... .
chapters.trap: Writing indicial roots ±ν² instead of ±ν, and forgetting the weight x in Bessel orthogonality.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 Frobenius; 3.1 regular singular points; Gamma function.
chapters.leave: Legendre polynomials are in 3.4; general Sturm-Liouville orthogonality is in 3.6.

chapters.idea: A second-order ODE can be put in self-adjoint Sturm-Liouville form, where eigenfunctions with the weight w are orthogonal and can be normalized.
chapters.depth: Cover self-adjoint form (p y')' + (q + λw)y = 0 with p > 0 and w > 0, plus separated boundary conditions. Show how to multiply a y'' + b y' + c y = 0 by an integrating factor to reach self-adjoint form. State Lagrange identity, real eigenvalues, and orthogonality ∫ w(x)y_m(x)y_n(x) dx = 0 for distinct eigenvalues. Define orthonormal system and characteristic functions (eigenfunctions). Give examples: y'' + λy = 0 with y(0) = y(π) = 0; Legendre with weight 1; Bessel with weight x. Some syllabi call this a Sturm-Liouville boundary value problem.

figure.aria: Three sine curves on zero to pi illustrate the orthogonal eigenfunctions of a Sturm-Liouville problem.

chapters.example: Solve y'' + λy = 0 with y(0) = 0 and y(π) = 0. Find all eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, and verify ∫_0^π sin x sin 2x dx = 0. The eigenvalues are λ_n = n² for n = 1, 2, 3, ... with eigenfunctions sin(nx); the integral is zero by direct integration or orthogonality.
chapters.trap: Using weight 1 when the problem has w(x) ≠ 1, and forgetting that the boundary conditions are part of the Sturm-Liouville problem.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 second-order ODEs; 3.4 and 3.5 for Legendre and Bessel examples.
chapters.leave: Oscillation and comparison of zeros are in 3.7; PDE eigenfunction expansions are in Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Abel's formula fixes the Wronskian, and Sturm theorems compare zeros of solutions: zeros of independent solutions separate, and larger q makes solutions oscillate faster.
chapters.depth: Give Abel's formula for y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = 0: W(x) = W(x0) exp(−∫_{x0}^{x} P(t) dt). State Sturm separation: zeros of two linearly independent solutions of the same ODE interlace. State Sturm comparison: for y'' + q1(x)y = 0 and y'' + q2(x)y = 0 with q1 ≥ q2, between consecutive zeros of a nontrivial solution of the q2 equation there is at least one zero of a nontrivial solution of the q1 equation. Use sin 2x and sin x. Some syllabi call this Sturm's fundamental comparison theorem. Only a few universities teach the proofs in detail.

figure.aria: Two sine curves show a zero of the faster sin two x falling between consecutive zeros of sin x.

chapters.example: Compare y'' + 4y = 0 with y'' + y = 0. Here q1 = 4 and q2 = 1, so q1 > q2. The slower solution y2 = sin x has consecutive zeros at x = 0 and x = π; the faster solution y1 = sin 2x has a zero at x = π/2 between them. Also, for y'' + y = 0 with y1 = sin x and y2 = cos x, W(0) = −1; use Abel's formula to find W(π/2). Since P = 0, W(π/2) = −1.
chapters.trap: Reversing Sturm comparison: larger q makes zeros more frequent, so compare between zeros of the slower solution. Abel gives W up to the exponential factor, not W constant unless P = 0.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 Wronskian and linear independence; 3.6 eigenfunctions; 3.4 and 3.5 zeros of Legendre and Bessel functions.
chapters.leave: Solving new ODEs, numerical zero finding, and PDE applications are outside this chapter.
